subject: turtle
reasoning:
I'm planning out a green sea turtle model — roughly 1.1 meters in shell length, resting on the ground with its belly near floor level and flippers extended outward. I'm starting to map out the skeleton structure, beginning with the root bone.

Then I'm designing the shell as two lofted shapes: a domed carapace on top and a flatter plastron underneath that sits at ground level, adjusting station widths and heights along the spine so the carapace tapers correctly at the front and back.

For coloring I'm using patch painting over the base olive shell tone to create a mottled scute pattern, plus a cream-colored plastron rim for contrast, skipping extra ridge details since the patches should read well enough on their own.

Now I'm setting up the skeletal structure, defining a spine chain of joints running from tail to front, parented under the hips root joint.

Still adding jaw joint and head parts...

Working out the flipper geometry...

Defining shorter, wider rear flippers with a tapered radius, plus a short tail stub between them with its own sweep. For the neck skin I'm layering a mottled olive base with a cream throat sector, and adding tiny claw spikes to the front flipper tips.

Now I'm adding keel scutes along the shell by sweeping small cones along the carapace loft at several points, and planning a rim detail along another line of the shell.

For the plastron, I'm setting up loft stations along the z-axis with varying widths to form the bottom shell shape, making sure it sits slightly narrower than the carapace to create a natural overhang, and adjusting the center height so the bottom surface lines up correctly at zero.

For texturing, I'm applying mottled paint patches in shell tones directly onto the carapace surface for a natural coloring effect, skipping countershading since it's not needed here. For the skeleton, I'm setting up a bone chain for the spine and plastron, then placing a small dark sphere as the eye pupil near the head bone, with mirroring handled by a sign multiplier. Finally I'm wrapping up with the export step.
